records.title: Popocatepetl and Iztaccihuatl: The Volcano Lovers
records.summary: Before the arrival of Europeans in the Valley of Mexico, the brave Tlaxcaltec warrior Popocatepetl fell deeply in love with the beautiful princess Iztaccihuatl. Before departing for war against the oppressive Aztec empire, the chieftain promised Popocatepetl his daughter's hand if he returned victorious. However, a jealous rival sent back false news that the warrior had fallen in battle. Overcome with inconsolable grief, Iztaccihuatl sickened and died. When Popocatepetl returned triumphant, he carried her body to the mountain heights, building a vast funeral pyre and kneeling with a burning torch to watch over her eternal slumber, transforming into the two iconic smoking volcanoes overlooking Mexico City.
alternate_names: The Legend of the Two Volcanoes
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica (recorded in colonial chronicles c. 16th Century)
records.region_or_community: Valley of Mexico and Puebla, Central Highlands

records.title: Quetzalcoatl and the Bones of Mankind
records.summary: Following the cosmic destruction of the previous worlds, the Feathered Serpent god Quetzalcoatl descends into Mictlan, the terrifying nine-layered underworld of the dead, to retrieve the sacred bones of past generations. The underworld ruler Mictlantecuhtli sets deceptive trials, demanding Quetzalcoatl blow a conch shell without finger holes. Enlisting worms and bees to bore through the shell, Quetzalcoatl completes the task and flees with the bones. Tricked into stumbling into a pit by Mictlantecuhtli's quails, the bones shatter into unequal fragments. Escaping to Tamoanchan, the goddess Quilaztli grinds the shards into meal, and the gods sprinkle their own blood over the powder to create diverse modern humanity.
alternate_names: The Creation of the Fifth Sun's People
records.historical_period: Classical Postclassic Mesoamerica (preserved in the Leyenda de los Soles, c. 1558)

records.title: The Discovery of Maize (Centli)
records.summary: In early times when humans ate only roots and wild game, the gods sought a sacred grain that would give strength and wisdom to the people of the sun. Quetzalcoatl noticed a small red ant carrying a golden kernel of corn (centli) across the stones. Transforming himself into a tiny black ant, Quetzalcoatl followed the creature deep into the cleft of Tonacatepetl, the Mountain of Sustenance. Navigating narrow crevices, he retrieved the golden seed and brought it to Tamoanchan, where the deities planted it. The god of rain, Tlaloc, split the mountain with lightning, allowing humanity to harvest the four colors of sacred maize: white, yellow, red, and black.
records.historical_period: Ancient Postclassic Era (codical compilation c. 16th Century)
records.region_or_community: Milpa Alta and Central Valley of Mexico

records.title: The Rabbit in the Moon (El Conejo en la Luna)
records.summary: Weary from wandering the earth in the mortal guise of a humble traveler, the benevolent god Quetzalcoatl sat beside the road as night fell, faint with hunger and thirst. A modest little rabbit emerged from the tall grass to nibble clover and noticed the traveler's exhaustion. When Quetzalcoatl explained that he had nothing to eat and might perish, the rabbit, knowing it was merely a frail creature, offered its own body as nourishment: 'I am only a little rabbit, but take me, roast me, and eat me so you may live.' Moved to tears by such boundless generosity, Quetzalcoatl lifted the rabbit high against the silver disc of the moon, stamping its silhouette across the lunar surface so that all humanity would remember its selflessness for eternity.
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica (recorded in early colonial chronicles)
records.region_or_community: Central Highlands of Mexico, Nahua oral traditions

records.title: The Legend of the Cempasuchil Flower
records.summary: Since childhood, Xochitl and Huitzilin shared a profound love, daily climbing a high hill to offer wild flowers to the sun god Tonatiuh. When war summoned Huitzilin to defend their people, the young warrior fell in battle. Shattered by grief, Xochitl prayed to Tonatiuh to reunite her with her beloved. Touched by her sorrow, the sun god cast a warm golden ray upon her; she dissolved into a fragrant, twenty-petaled golden flower (cempasúchil). Soon after, a hummingbird—the reincarnated spirit of Huitzilin—fluttered down and drank nectar from its heart, causing the blossom to unfurl in radiant orange hues, guiding departed souls on Dia de los Muertos.
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Nahua Tradition (foundational to Dia de los Muertos culture)
records.region_or_community: Puebla, Tlaxcala, and Valley of Mexico

records.title: The Eagle on the Nopal: Foundation of Tenochtitlan
records.summary: Led by their tribal patron god Huitzilopochtli, the Mexica wandered for over two centuries through the harsh northern deserts seeking a promised homeland. The god decreed that they must settle only where they witnessed a divine sign: a golden eagle perched atop a prickly pear cactus (nopal) growing out of a stone, devouring a serpent. In 1325, upon arriving at the swampy, reed-filled shores of Lake Texcoco, the priests sighted the majestic eagle spreading its wings in the marshy waters. Founding their capital Mexico-Tenochtitlan upon the island, the sacred vision became the eternal emblem of the Mexican nation and flag.
records.historical_period: Postclassic Era (c. 1325 CE foundation, recorded in Codex Mendoza)
records.region_or_community: Lake Texcoco basin, Valley of Mexico

records.title: The Nagual Shapeshifter of Oaxaca
records.summary: In the indigenous Zapotec, Mixtec, and Nahua communities of Oaxaca and southern Mexico, a nagual (nahual) is a powerful shaman or sorcerer who possesses the supernatural ability to shed their human form at night and take the shape of an animal companion, such as a black jaguar, owl, feral dog, or serpent. Linked to an individual's astrological birth day (tonal), an ethical nagual uses their vision to protect community boundaries and heal ailments, while malevolent naguales enter rural corrals to steal livestock or cast hexes. The folklore reflects deep Mesoamerican concepts of dual consciousness and animal co-essences.
records.region_or_community: Central Valleys and Sierra Juárez, Oaxaca

records.title: The Creation of the Fifth Sun at Teotihuacan
records.summary: Gathered in primordial darkness at the sacred city of Teotihuacan, the gods determined that one of them must sacrifice himself in a colossal divine pyre (teotexcalli) to create a new sun. The wealthy, proud god Tecuciztecatl volunteered, offering precious feathers and jade, while the humble, diseased god Nanahuatzin offered humble thorns and his own blood. When the bonfire blazed, Tecuciztecatl hesitated in terror four times before the blistering flames. Nanahuatzin, fearless in devotion, closed his eyes and leaped into the inferno, rising into the heavens as the blazing sun Tonatiuh. Shamed, Tecuciztecatl jumped in afterward, becoming the paler moon.
records.historical_period: Classical Teotihuacan / Aztec Cosmogony (recorded in Florentine Codex Book VII)

records.title: The Singing Maiden of Lake Chapala
records.summary: Lake Chapala, Mexico's largest freshwater lake in Jalisco, is revered in Coca and Wixárika (Huichol) cosmology as a sacred body of water governed by the mother goddess of water, Xapawiyemeka. Traditional folklore tells of a beautiful indigenous maiden who threw herself into the lake during the Spanish conquest to avoid capture by conquistadors. On quiet moonlit evenings when mist blankets the reeds of Mezcala Island, fishermen hear her sweet, melancholic singing floating across the gentle swells, warning boaters of sudden squalls and blessing their nets with abundant whitefish.
records.historical_period: Colonial Era to Present (tradition spanning indigenous Wixárika rituals)

records.title: The Crying Tree of the Sad Night (Noche Triste)
records.summary: On the rainy night of June 30, 1520, Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and his surviving soldiers fled Mexico-Tenochtitlan along the Tlacopan causeway after a fierce Mexica counter-offensive decimated their ranks. Exhausted and bleeding, Cortés collapsed beneath the sprawling boughs of an ancient Montezuma cypress (ahuehuete) in Popotla and wept openly over the catastrophic loss of his men and plunder, an event commemorated in Mexican history as La Noche Triste (The Sad Night). For centuries, the charred trunk of the sacred tree stood as a living monument to indigenous resistance and Spanish defeat.
alternate_names: El Árbol de la Noche Triste
records.region_or_community: Popotla, Mexico City (now Miguel Hidalgo borough)
